Tollgate Neighbourhood Association
For our members and the Maddersby Town Council Resilience Fund

Summary

Between Monday 15 June and Sunday 13 September 2026, Tollgate Neighbourhood Association (TNA) ran Cool Rooms at three sites on hot days and offered phone check-ins to residents who asked for them. There were 27 heat days. Across 72 site openings we recorded 1,239 visits. We also made 1,311 scheduled check-ins, and 38 trained volunteers took on at least one shift or call round. Volunteers gave 684 recorded hours.

There is much to build on, and there are clear things to put right. Our leaflets went out after the first heat day, nine possible site openings were missed, 11 room shifts had only one volunteer, and some visitors told us that publicity or transport made it harder to come, or to come sooner. At 31 October, £1,270 was unspent. Whether any council money within that sum can be carried forward has not been settled.

What we set out to do

In March 2026 the committee agreed the aim: to give people in Tollgate ward a free, cool and welcoming place to sit on hot days, with drinking water, and to offer a phone check-in to residents who asked for one. Visitors needed no referral, booking or proof of address.

The Cool Rooms are not a medical service, and volunteers do not give medical advice. If someone seems unwell, volunteers follow our safeguarding sheet and call for help.

How it worked

A heat day was one with a forecast maximum of 28°C or above for Maddersby. The three host sites were St Orrin's Church Hall on Pell Street, the meeting room at Tollgate Branch Library, and Kettle Yard Community Centre. The usual hours on heat days were 11am to 6pm. Our rule was that every room shift should have at least two volunteers.

The season had five heat days in June, 11 in July, nine in August and two in September. Four of them fell on Sundays: 5 and 12 July, and 2 and 9 August.

When the rooms were open

Not every site was open on every heat day. Had all three opened each time, there would have been 81 site openings. We achieved 72.

St Orrin's opened on 25 heat days. It was closed on 24 June and 14 August because the hall was booked for funerals.

The library opened on 23 heat days. It does not open on Sundays, so it missed all four Sunday heat days, leaving no more than two sites open on each of those days.

Kettle Yard opened on 24 heat days. Its air-conditioning broke down, and the room was closed on 21, 22 and 23 July. The repair was completed on 24 July, and the room reopened that day. The centre manager could not say whether an earlier service would have prevented the fault.

The Kettle Yard closure included our busiest day. We had no agreed back-up room and no clear way of telling people that the site was shut. A handwritten sign went on the door, and callers mentioned the closure to people they spoke to.

Visits

We count a visit as one person arriving at one site on one day. Someone who came on ten days therefore counts as ten visits. We did not require names, so we do not know how many different people used the rooms. Some 214 people left a first name and postcode at least once, but because this was voluntary, it is not a count of everyone who came.

By site, the totals were:

• Library: 538 visits from 23 openings, an average of 23.4 per opening.
• St Orrin's: 412 visits from 25 openings, an average of 16.5.
• Kettle Yard: 289 visits from 24 openings, an average of 12.0.

Across all sites, the average was 17.2 visits per opening.

By month, we recorded 168 visits in June, 561 in July, 437 in August and 73 in September. These monthly totals reflect differences in the number of heat days and site openings, as well as in attendance.

The busiest day was Tuesday 21 July, with 96 visits: 57 at the library and 39 at St Orrin's. Kettle Yard was closed.

Tally sheets were filled in differently between sites during the first week. Our volunteer lead, Dev Ransome, then issued a single sheet. The visit figures are our best count.

Life in the rooms

Volunteers felt that asking no questions at the door helped people to feel comfortable. Several noticed regular visitors getting to know one another, with some staying to chat or play cards.

The library was our busiest room. Its branch manager, Bea Lindqvist, thought this was partly because people already knew the building. That is her impression; we did not ask visitors why they chose a site. Seating was tight on the hottest afternoons, and the children's corner shares the room with the seating, so quiet and play competed for space. Library staff often answered questions about the scheme when no TNA volunteer was free. Site notes also record that visitors raised the Sunday closure more than once.

At St Orrin's, volunteers set up a cold water table by the Pell Street door. It was popular, and people passing could use it without coming in. They were not counted as visits. The hall stayed reasonably cool in the morning but warmed by mid-afternoon, when the portable cooling units helped. Volunteers would like more chairs with arms.

Kettle Yard was a quieter site with a good kitchen for refilling water jugs. Volunteers think its entrance is hard to find from the main road and suggest an outdoor sign. The committee has not yet discussed this.

Phone check-ins

In all, 57 residents signed up for calls on heat days, and call rounds took place on every one of those days. Not everyone was on the list for the whole season, and some paused their calls while away.

Of 1,311 scheduled check-ins, 1,302 reached the resident within three tries. The other nine were followed up. Seven were settled by a neighbour or a volunteer visit; on the other two occasions, emergency services were called. To protect residents' privacy, we are not publishing any circumstances.

Our safeguarding lead, Ottoline Marsh, reported that the three-tries rule worked as intended. We cannot say what would have happened without the calls or the rooms, and we make no claim about that.

Most calls were short. Some residents enjoyed a longer chat, which meant rounds took more time. Callers would also like the list to be updated more promptly when residents say they will be away.

Our volunteers

We held training on Saturday 30 May and Saturday 6 June. Of the 46 people trained, 38 did at least one room shift or call round.

The 684 recorded hours were divided as follows: 236 on shifts at St Orrin's, 214 at the library, 198 at Kettle Yard and 36 on check-in calls. These figures come from signed rota sheets. They leave out planning meetings, shopping and leaflet delivery.

Despite this commitment, 11 room shifts were covered by only one person, below our minimum of two. Late notice was the main complaint from volunteers: we sometimes confirmed a heat day only that morning.

What visitors told us

Visitors returned 112 voluntary paper forms across the three sites. Some people may have completed more than one, so the numbers below refer to forms and should not be read as a count of different people. Forms were not offered to people who only received phone calls, and the results may not represent everyone who used the programme.

On 64 forms, the respondent was aged 65 or over. On 41, the respondent reported having no fan or other cooling at home.

Asked whether they would use a Cool Room again, 89 forms said yes (about 79%), 17 said not sure and six gave no answer. None said no.

On how people first heard about the rooms, 42 forms named a neighbour or friend, 33 a leaflet, 19 library staff and seven a poster at a GP surgery. The remaining 11 gave another source or no answer.

People could also tick things that had made it harder to come, or to come sooner; many left this blank. Not knowing about the rooms early enough was ticked on 37 forms, and getting there or transport on 18.

These anonymous comments were checked by our safeguarding lead as safe to quote:

“My flat holds the heat all night. A few hours somewhere cool made the day manageable.”

“I came for the water and stayed for the company.”

“I didn't know it was for me. I thought you had to be referred.”

“The bus doesn't go near enough when it's that hot.”

“Somewhere quiet to sit would help. The children's corner was lovely but loud.”

What we need to improve

Publicity was late. Leaflets did not go out until Friday 19 June, the day after our first heat day, so we had opened before most households had one. The wording was not signed off until the second week of June, and printing then took a further week.

The message also needed to be clearer. The front of the leaflet did not say that no referral was needed. Volunteers heard at the door the same misunderstanding that appears in one of the comments above.

Transport remains a concern. Volunteers gave examples of people finding the walk difficult in the heat. We do not know how many people stayed away altogether because of travel.

Alongside this, we need to address Sunday cover, plans for unexpected closures, notice for volunteers, thin rotas, quiet space and consistent record keeping.

Money

Income totalled £9,635: £6,500 from the Town Council Resilience Fund, £2,000 from Fennick Housing Trust and £1,135 in donations.

Spending to 31 October was £8,365, against a budget of £8,600:

• Venue hire: £3,240 (budget £3,500)
• Portable cooling units and fans: £2,415 (budget £2,500)
• Water and refreshments: £1,186 (budget £1,000)
• Printing and leaflets: £512 (budget £450)
• Insurance add-on: £450 (budget £450)
• Volunteer expenses: £368 (budget £500)
• Phone credit: £194 (budget £200)

Although total spending was within budget, water and refreshments, and printing and leaflets, each went over their budget lines. The portable units and fans are now in storage and can be used again, subject to checks.

The unspent balance is £1,270. Under the council grant condition, unspent council money must be returned by 31 December 2026, or carried forward with the council's written permission by that date. The treasurer has not yet worked out how much of the balance counts as council money, and we have not received permission to carry any forward. We therefore cannot assume that the full balance will be available in 2027.

Looking ahead to 2027

Agreed actions

The season debrief on 8 October agreed five actions:

1. The decision to open will be made and sent to volunteers by 4pm the day before. If the forecast changes late, we will still open if the morning forecast reaches the threshold. (Marnie Okafor-Hale)
2. All new volunteers will receive the safeguarding briefing before their first shift. (Ottoline Marsh)
3. All sites will use one shared tally sheet from the first day. (Dev Ransome)
4. Leaflets are to be delivered by 1 June 2027, with “Free. No referral or booking needed” on the front. Delivery depends on printing funds being in place. (Marnie Okafor-Hale)
5. Kettle Yard will arrange an air-conditioning service in May 2027. (Samuel Adeyemi-Cross, centre manager)

Proposals and open questions

The following points have not been decided.

• Season dates: the proposal is Monday 14 June to Sunday 12 September 2027.
• Opening threshold: one suggestion is to keep 28°C for now and look at a rule for very warm nights. Some volunteers want to open after such nights; others worry about stretching the rota.
• Sunday cover: Sunday opening at the library is not possible under current staffing. A volunteer suggested looking for another venue, but none has been approached.
• Closures: one idea is to name a back-up room before the season and agree how closures will be announced. No room has been identified.
• Volunteers: the volunteer lead proposes aiming for 55 trained volunteers.
• Transport: the coordinator is to make first enquiries with Maddersby Dial-a-Ride. We have no agreement or cost from the service.
• Quiet space: the library branch manager will look at whether the layout can be changed, with no promise that it can.

The treasurer has prepared a draft 2027 budget of £8,900. It comprises £3,600 for venue hire, £1,400 for water and refreshments, £1,150 for a transport trial, £900 for equipment checks and replacements, £600 for printing and leaflets, £500 for volunteer expenses, £500 for insurance and £250 for phone credit. The committee has not approved it, and no 2027 funding has been confirmed from any source. The committee is due to consider the draft budget and open items on 9 December 2026.

Thank you

Thank you to every volunteer who welcomed visitors, covered a shift or made calls. We are grateful to our three host sites, and to library staff for pointing visitors to the room. St Orrin's has said it was glad to take part and wishes to be involved again, although funeral bookings will always take priority.

Thank you also to the Maddersby Town Council Resilience Fund, Fennick Housing Trust and everyone who donated.

Marnie Okafor-Hale, Programme Coordinator, Tollgate Neighbourhood Association

FENNICK STREET TOOL LIBRARY - OPERATIONS NOTES (running document)
Kept by Rosalind. Last tidied 18 November 2026. This is a dumping ground for how we actually do things. One day it will become a proper guide.

1. WHO WE ARE
We are a member-run lending library for tools, based in the old print works unit at the bottom of Fennick Street. Members borrow tools the way people borrow books. The point is that nobody should have to buy a drill they will use twice a year. We also run a small repair workshop where volunteers keep the stock in working order. The workshop is not a public repair service. People sometimes ask us to fix their toaster. We say no, kindly, and mention that we only maintain our own stock.

Current people and what they look after:
- Rosalind Achterberg, Operations Coordinator. Rota, inductions, policies, anything to do with staff and volunteers.
- Tobiah Mensah-Reid, Workshop Lead. Repairs, safety checks, deciding whether a tool goes back on the shelf.
- Priyanka Oduya, Membership and Money. Sign-ups, fees, refunds, fee waivers, the cash box.
- Gil Fairweather, Chair of the committee. Complaints that cannot be settled at the desk, and anything involving press or the landlord.

2. OPENING HOURS
Tuesday 14:00 to 20:00
Wednesday 10:00 to 16:00
Thursday 14:00 to 20:00
Saturday 09:00 to 15:00
Closed Sunday, Monday and Friday. Friday is often used by Tobiah for big repair jobs, but the doors stay locked to members.
People on the first shift of the day should arrive 30 minutes before opening. The last people out usually need about 30 minutes after closing.
Nobody is ever alone in the building during opening hours. Minimum is two people, and at least one of them must be a keyholder. If you are the only one there at opening time, keep the door locked and ring Rosalind.

3. OPENING UP
Keyholder unlocks the side door (the front shutter sticks, don't try to lift it from inside until the side door is open and the shutter bolt is off).
Alarm: keyholders get the code from Rosalind in person. It is never written in this document, never texted.
Lights: the switches are behind the returns shelf. The workshop has its own switch by the workshop door.
Turn on the desk laptop and the barcode scanner. The scanner takes a minute to pair. If it won't pair, switch it off and on again before doing anything cleverer.
Check the quarantine shelf (red tape) and make sure nothing has wandered off it onto the lending shelves.
Walk the floor: check fire exits are clear, especially the back one near the ladder rack, which gets blocked by returns.
Put the A-board out on the pavement. Keep it against the wall so wheelchairs and prams can pass.
Count the cash float. It should be 40 pounds. If it is not, write the amount in the cash book and tell Priyanka the same day. Do not top it up from your own pocket.

4. MEMBERSHIP
Anyone aged 18 or over who lives or works in the local area can join. Ask for photo ID and one proof of address or workplace dated within the last three months. We look at the documents, we do not photocopy or photograph them.
Annual fee: 30 pounds standard. 12 pounds concession. We do not ask people to prove they qualify for concession. If they say so, they get it.
Fee waivers: some people cannot pay even the concession. Desk staff do not decide this and should not make anyone explain their situation at the counter. Say that waivers exist and pass the person's name and preferred contact method to Priyanka.
Every new member reads and signs the borrowing agreement before their first loan. No exceptions, including friends of volunteers.

5. LOANS
Standard loan is 7 days.
Up to 5 items at a time.
One renewal of 7 days is allowed if nobody has reserved the item. Renewals can be done in person, by phone or by email.
Reservations: members can reserve an item for a set start date. Reserved items go on the blue shelf with a slip showing the member's surname and the date.
Some tools need a short induction before a member can borrow them: chainsaws are not stocked at all, but the following ARE stocked and DO need induction: the tile cutter, the mitre saw, the pressure washer and the floor sander. Only Tobiah or a volunteer he has signed off can give a tool induction. The member record shows which inductions each person has. **Only Tobiah or a signed-off repair volunteer may take anything off the quarantine shelf.** Desk volunteers can't, and neither can anyone else without that authority, even if the fault looks trivial or already fixed.

Twice this autumn, someone trying to help moved a tagged tool back to the main shelves. One was a hedge trimmer with a damaged cable. Nobody was hurt, but please never move tagged items back.

## Working in the workshop

**Anyone may say stop if something looks unsafe, whether it's their first day or their tenth year. Work then stops while we look.**

Don't use any workshop machine until you've had your induction with Tobiah.

- Wear eye protection at the bench grinder and for any cutting, and ear defenders for anything loud. Both are on the pegboard by the door.
- Tie back long hair and wear closed shoes. Keep loose sleeves, lanyards and dangling jewellery away from rotating tools.
- Don't wear gloves at the bench grinder or pillar drill.
- Never run a powered tool in the workshop unless someone else is in the building and knows you're there.
- Unplug a tool before changing a blade or opening its casing.
- Pass any electrical repair beyond changing a plug or fuse to Tobiah.
- Put swollen, damaged or hot batteries in the metal bin with sand outside the back door. Never charge a damaged battery.
- Never leave anything charging when the building is locked. This includes the card reader, so charge it during opening hours.
- Sweep and empty the dust extractor at the end of each session.

After your induction, you'll work on repairs alongside Tobiah or another signed-off volunteer. Tobiah signs you off when he's happy; there is no fixed number of sessions. When you finish a repair, write what you did on the fault tag and keep the tag for Tobiah to file. The item can leave quarantine only after it passes a test run, and only with Tobiah or a signed-off repair volunteer.

If you're unsure, leave the item on the bench with a note and ask Tobiah. Nobody gets told off for asking.

## Fire, first aid and incidents

**In a fire,** shout, get people out and call 999 from outside. Don't go back for tools or the laptop. Meet at the lamp post opposite the bakery shutter, across the road. If the sign-in sheet is on your way out, take it so we can count heads. Only use an extinguisher on a tiny fire if you've been shown how. Getting out comes first.

Everyone on shift signs in on arrival and out on leaving, as do workshop visitors.

The main first aid kit is on the wall behind the desk, with a smaller one in the workshop.

Record every accident and near miss in the green incident book under the desk on the same day, and tell Rosalind. Near misses help us find problems before someone gets hurt.

## Difficult moments

You never have to win an argument. Stay calm, listen and repeat back what you've understood. Don't promise a refund, waiver or exception. Explain who will look at it (Priyanka for money, Tobiah for tool condition) and add a note to the member's record. The member involved in the October late fee row has since settled up, and Priyanka has the details.

If someone is abusive or makes you feel unsafe, you can end the conversation. Get your shift partner. If anyone is in immediate danger, call 999. Record it in the incident book and tell Rosalind, who will involve Gil if it needs to go further.

## Money, donations and privacy

We prefer card payments, but cash is fine. Write every cash payment in the cash book and offer a receipt. Mark money donations as 'donation' in the book. Only Priyanka gives refunds.

Before accepting a donated tool, check the wanted list on the noticeboard. If it's listed, fill in a donation slip and put it on the quarantine shelf, because we treat all donations as untested. If it isn't listed, politely ask the donor to email us a photo first. We never accept petrol-powered tools or fuel of any kind.

Lock the laptop screen whenever you step away. Don't read out addresses or phone numbers across the room. Never reveal who has borrowed a tool, even to a member waiting for it. Just give the expected return date.

## Closing down

Stop new loans 10 minutes before closing. Then:

- Count the cash box and write the total in the cash book. Leave the £40 float and put any extra in the safe envelope with the date and your initials.
- Check that workshop machines are unplugged, chargers are off and the extractor is empty.
- Bring in the A-board.
- Check that the toilets and back room are empty.
- Bolt the back door, then lower and bolt the shutter.
- Sign out. The keyholder sets the alarm and locks the side door.

## Finally

A printed copy of this guide will be at [location of the printed copy]. If anything here is unclear, ask Rosalind. You can also drop in during her office hours on Wednesday mornings. Welcome to the team.

Dem Vorstand liegt ein Angebot der Firma Rohrbau Hellkamp über 18.640 EUR für die Erneuerung des Hauptstrangs vor. Ein Teil der Kosten wird aus der Rücklage bezahlt, der Rest über eine einmalige Umlage.

Die Arbeiten sollen ab dem 8. März 2027 beginnen und etwa drei Wochen dauern. Die Wege müssen im Bereich der Leitung frei zugänglich sein. Lagerungen am Wegrand (Erde, Holz, Steine) sind bis zum 28. Februar 2027 zu entfernen.

Betreff: Unser Angebot Nr. 2026-118 zur Einrichtung des Kinder- und Ausleihbereichs

Sehr geehrte Frau Wendland,

vielen Dank für das Gespräch bei unserem Vor-Ort-Termin am 12. November. Anbei erhalten Sie unser Angebot Nr. 2026-118 vom 24. November 2026 für die Einrichtung des Kinder- und Ausleihbereichs der Gemeindebücherei Erlenbrück.

Sie möchten den Kinderbereich offener gestalten, und die Kinder sollen selbst an die Bilderbücher kommen. Dafür sehen wir vier Bilderbuchtröge aus Birke Multiplex vor. Da sie rollbar sind, lässt sich für Vorlesestunden Platz schaffen. Die Sitznische mit gepolsterter Bank ist für den Platz unter dem Fenster an der Südseite gedacht und bietet Stauraum für Sitzkissen. Die Ausleihtheke erhält einen abgesenkten Abschnitt, der für Kinder und für Menschen im Rollstuhl gut erreichbar sein soll. Hinzu kommen sechs Wandregale aus geölter, massiver Eiche, die kippsicher verankert werden. Die Wand im Altbau habe ich mir beim Termin angesehen: Eine Befestigung ist möglich.

Die Zwischensumme einschließlich Lieferung und Montage beträgt [Zwischensumme netto nach Korrektur des Angebots] zuzüglich der gesetzlichen Umsatzsteuer. Die Fertigung dauert ab Ihrer schriftlichen Auftragserteilung etwa acht Wochen, für die Montage rechnen wir mit voraussichtlich zwei Tagen. Gern legen wir diese auf Schließtage, damit der Büchereibetrieb nicht gestört wird. Die genauen Termine stimmen wir noch mit Ihnen ab.

Bitte beachten Sie, dass die Entsorgung der alten Regale nicht im Angebot enthalten ist. Sie wollten mit dem Bauhof klären, ob er diese abholt.

Bei Auftragserteilung werden 30 % fällig, der Restbetrag ist innerhalb von 14 Tagen nach der Abnahme zu zahlen. Das Angebot ist bis zum 18. Dezember 2026 gültig.

Wenn Sie sich die Materialien vorab ansehen möchten, bringe ich Ihnen bei Bedarf gern Muster der geölten Eiche und des Birke Multiplex vorbei. Auch für Fragen zum Angebot stehe ich Ihnen gern zur Verfügung. Ich freue mich auf Ihre Rückmeldung.

Mit freundlichen Grüßen
Jonas Feldkamp
Tischlerei Feldkamp
